newCard.subject: Geography
newCard.name: Ontario’s major landform regions
newCard.description: Identify the broad Ontario locations and distinguishing landscape characteristics of the Canadian Shield, Hudson Bay Lowland and Great Lakes–St. Lawrence Lowlands using the stated current physical-region convention. Distinguish these physical regions from provincial or community boundaries, and recognize that each broad region includes local variation.
evidence: Name and indicate the broad Ontario locations of the Canadian Shield, Hudson Bay Lowland and Great Lakes–St. Lawrence Lowlands on an outline/reference map.

Describe distinguishing characteristics: the Shield’s widespread rock, rounded terrain and many lakes; the Hudson Bay Lowland’s low-relief wetland plain near Hudson and James bays; and the southern Great Lakes–St. Lawrence plain-like lowlands with local hills and an escarpment.

Recognize the same regional pattern on a differently styled map and explain why physical-region boundaries are not simply province or community boundaries; do not treat a broad region as completely uniform.
newCard.assessmentPrompt: After exploring the current physical-region map together with an Ontario outline, show {{name}} an Ontario outline with major waters but without the three region names. Can they name the three broad physical regions from the convention you studied, show their broad locations and explain a characteristic that distinguishes each? Ask whether every location within one region must look identical, and have them explain using a checked Ontario example. Then use a differently styled reference map: can they recognize the same regions without relying on one colour scheme or confusing them with province or community boundaries?

pedagogy.summary: Build a bounded regional knowledge pattern using the current physical-region convention and a separately identified provincial reference. Link names and broad locations to distinguishing characteristics rather than teaching a colour key or a uniform stereotype.
bestPractices: Pair the current NRCan physical-region map with the verified Ontario outline. Their layers answer different questions; do not relabel a political boundary as a physical-region boundary.

Use Ontario examples where supplied: the Attawapiskat River low-relief wetland setting and the Niagara Escarpment within the southern lowlands. Do not relabel Manitoba or Quebec photographs as Ontario.
Ask for the three names and distinguishing characteristics after study, then transfer across map styling; do not certify regional knowledge solely by reading supplied labels.
keyRepresentations: Current Atlas physical-region map and its stated legend
Separately attributed Ontario provincial outline, with major waters used as reference
Original short regional comparisons grounded in the checked descriptions
commonMisconceptions: Every lowland is perfectly flat or the same as every other lowland.
The same boundary divides physical regions, provinces and First Nations communities.
A region is its colour on one particular map.

learn.summary: Connect each name, its broad location and a distinguishing landscape pattern, retaining both local variation and the difference between political and physical reference layers.

activities.title: One province, three broad physical patterns
learnerActions: Find Ontario on the Statistics Canada reference and relate its major-water outline to the current NRCan national physical map. Identify the legend and keep political and physical boundaries distinct.
Locate and name the three Ontario-relevant broad regions using the stated current convention; compare their landscape descriptions rather than memorizing colours.

Use the Ontario Attawapiskat River example for the northern low-relief wetland and the Niagara Escarpment description to challenge the idea that southern lowlands have no relief. Describe the Shield’s rock-and-lake pattern without claiming every location is identical.
Remove the region-name labels from the assessment outline, explain locations and characteristics, then try a differently styled map with the same convention.
activities.intendedInsight: Named physical regions capture broad contrasting landscape patterns across Ontario; they do not simply reproduce political boundaries, and a broad region can contain local differences.
feedback: If the whole province is named Shield, return to the distinct northern wetland and southern lowland areas in the current physical layer.
If a lowland is called featureless or every wet area is treated as the same region, compare the stated descriptions and broad positions.
If a map colour or a provincial border supplies the answer, change the styling and name the source layer that actually represents physical regions.
activities.rationale: Original untested teaching proposal based on checked factual maps/text. Contrasts and changed-style transfer are designed to reveal regional knowledge rather than copied labels; no classroom intervention study is claimed.
sourceClaims: The current Atlas distinguishes Canadian Shield, Hudson Bay Lowland and Great Lakes–St. Lawrence Lowlands as physical regions with different landscape characteristics; the text gives an Ontario Hudson Bay Lowland example at the Attawapiskat River and southern lowland relief around the Niagara Escarpment.
Statistics Canada’s Ontario reference map identifies the provincial outline within Canada; it is a political reference, not a physical-region or Indigenous territory map.

constraints: Use broad educational placement, not a precise parcel, navigation, legal or Indigenous-territory boundary determination. Do not project current boundaries back onto1780–1850 maps.

The current national map has no provincial outline overlay; keep the paired verified provincial reference explicit. Do not manufacture precision by casually stretching or aligning different map images.
State the current three-region Ontario convention. The archived sixth-edition map has different Hudson/Shield subdivision terminology and is not an interchangeable working map.
No required geology formation chronology, mineral classification, exhaustive subregion inventory, ecozone equivalence, job pattern or environmental causal model is added.
Names may be said aloud and supplied place labels read aloud; spelling or a particular digital app is not assessed. No travel is required.
Elicit names and distinguishing characteristics before offering the worked comparison. Hints or repeated source labels are scaffolding, not independent evidence for the full knowledge claim.
reviewNotes: 2026-11-10: original source-checked factual proposal, reviewed for this bounded shared claim. Actual current region-layer image and the separate Statistics Canada provincial image were visually inspected. Earlier close-scale map export was blank outside the layer’s visibility range, not evidence of absent regions. Low confidence concerns untested teaching efficacy.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: After exploring the current physical-region map together with an Ontario outline, show {{name}} an Ontario outline with major waters but without the three region names. Can they name the three broad physical regions from the convention you studied, show their broad locations and explain a characteristic that distinguishes each? Ask whether every location within one region must look identical, and have them explain using a checked Ontario example. Then use a differently styled reference map: can they recognize the same regions without relying on one colour scheme or confusing them with province or community boundaries?
assess.correctAnswer: Names and broadly locates the three regions, explains their contrasting landscape characteristics, retains local variation and identifies the physical-layer versus political-boundary distinction on a new map.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: An outline without the three labels requires regional knowledge rather than copying. A northern wetland versus southern lowland comparison rules out a single undifferentiated lowland label, the escarpment challenges perfectly-flat reasoning, and changed styling rules out one colour key as the learned content.
probeDeeper: Which region’s broad pattern is shown here, and what feature supports your answer?
How can a lowland include an escarpment or hills?
Does this line show a province or a physical region, and how do you know?

errorPatterns.pattern: Names the entire province Shield or confuses political and physical layers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses Ontario’s provincial outline as the boundary of one physical region.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the separately labelled source layers and locate their distinct northern and southern areas before naming them again.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats both lowlands as identical and completely flat, or answers only by map colour.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot explain a distinguishing characteristic or loses the region when styling changes.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the source descriptions, contrast their setting and the southern escarpment example, then retry with different map colours.

responseLevels.gap: Does not identify the three broad regional names/patterns or substitutes political labels.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls names or one map but cannot distinguish their characteristics, local variation or changed styling.
responseLevels.full: Connects names, broad locations and distinguishing characteristics across the stated convention and a new styled map without equating political and physical boundaries.

existingCandidates.subject: Science
existingCandidates.name: Shapes of land and water
existingCandidates.description: Develop a model to represent the shapes and kinds of land (mountains, valleys, plains) and bodies of water (rivers, lakes, oceans) in an area
evidence: Name and describe at least four types of landforms (mountain, valley, plain, hill, cliff)
Name and describe at least three types of water bodies (river, lake, ocean, pond)
Create or interpret a simple model or map showing land and water features of an area
existingCandidates.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look at a map or build a model showing mountains, rivers, and oceans, and explain what each type of land or water feature is?

existingCandidates.subject: Geography
existingCandidates.name: Natural, managed and built features
existingCandidates.description: Identify the natural, managed and constructed features of local places and describe their location
evidence: Sort photos of local features into natural (creek, hill), managed (park, farm, garden) and constructed (road, school, shops)
Locate local places on a simple map of the neighbourhood and describe where they are with position words (e.g. 'the park is next to the library')
Explain why a park is a managed feature (people plant and look after it) even though it contains natural plants
existingCandidates.assessmentPrompt: On a walk around your neighbourhood, can {{name}} point out natural things like a creek, looked-after places like a park, and built things like roads and shops?

existingCandidates.subject: Geography
existingCandidates.name: Local, regional and state scales
existingCandidates.description: Represent places at different geographical scales (local, regional and state, territory or national) on maps, and describe how people and places are interconnected across those scales (e.g. through food, jobs, services and transport)
evidence: Locate their suburb or town, its region and their state or territory on a set of maps at different scales
Label the state or territory capital and one regional centre on a map of their state or territory
Trace an interconnection across scales (e.g. milk from a regional dairy farm to a local shop, or travelling to a city hospital) and draw it as a flow map
existingCandidates.assessmentPrompt: Looking at a map with {{name}}, can they find your suburb or town, your region and your state — and explain how things like food travel from farms to your local shop?

existingCandidates.subject: Geography
existingCandidates.name: Comparing places in different countries
existingCandidates.description: Compare the natural, managed and constructed features of places in their own country and in neighbouring or other countries (e.g. Australia and its neighbours)
evidence: Compare photos of an Australian place and a place in a neighbouring country (e.g. a Queensland coastal town and a village in Papua New Guinea) and list the natural, managed and constructed features of each
Record similarities and differences in a table or Venn diagram
Explain one reason for a difference (e.g. climate, landforms or how people use the land)
existingCandidates.assessmentPrompt: Looking at photos of a town in Australia and one in a nearby country like Papua New Guinea or Indonesia, can {{name}} spot what's similar and what's different?

existingCandidates.subject: Science
existingCandidates.name: Minerals and Earth resources
existingCandidates.description: Compare the observable properties of minerals (colour, lustre, scratch hardness) and investigate why soils, rocks and minerals are important Earth resources (building materials, growing food, metals, salt)
evidence: Compare minerals such as quartz, mica and halite by colour, lustre and a scratch test for hardness, recording results in a table
Match Earth resources to uses (e.g. clay to bricks, sand to glass, iron ore to steel, soil to growing food, salt to cooking)
Explain why one Earth resource is important to people in Australia (e.g. iron ore mining or soil for farming)
existingCandidates.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a rock or crystal collection, can they compare things like shininess and hardness — and explain how rocks, soils and minerals are used, like clay for bricks?

independentAssessmentBoundary: A learner may name general mountains/valleys/plains or use a familiar map without knowing Ontario’s actual regional names, positions and contrasting patterns. Conversely, regional knowledge does not prove general map construction or every landform operation. This is specific geographical knowledge, not a lower-difficulty duplicate.

sourceVerification.currentPhysicalMap: Actual current NRCan national Regions layer and its text/legend read and image visually inspected. The three Ontario-relevant regional names and pattern are retained using that stated convention.
sourceVerification.pairedProvince: Actual Statistics Canada Ontario outline image visually inspected; source page dated2017-09-28. It is a separate political reference, not a physical-region layer or legal survey.
sourceVerification.conventionLimits: The archived sixth-edition map uses different Hudson/Shield subdivision terminology. It was inspected as a historical convention check, not substituted for the current working map.
sourceVerification.scaleToolingLimit: The current Regions layer is visible only within its configured scale range. An earlier too-close export was blank; the successful national layer render supplied the visual check. No blanket source-access failure or missing region is inferred.
sourceVerification.projectionLimits: Keep the physical and provincial references separate. Do not stretch/align distinct images into a falsely precise overlay or treat physical boundaries as municipal/Indigenous jurisdiction.
